fixed_stress_answers.text: The five permanent members of the UN Security Council (the 'P5') are a complete, closed set: (1) China (People's Republic of China), (2) France, (3) Russia (Russian Federation), (4) the United Kingdom, and (5) the United States. This is fixed by Article 23(1) of the UN Charter (1945), which states the Council 'shall consist of fifteen Members' and names the permanent members; the original text lists the 'Republic of China' and the 'Union of Soviet Socialist Republics,' whose seats are now held by the People's Republic of China and the Russian Federation. Each of the five holds veto power over non-procedural decisions. The list is exhaustive at exactly five [doc1_un_charter_ch5; doc2_un_dag_library; doc3_wikipedia_p5].

ground_truth.answer: There are exactly five permanent members (the 'P5') of the United Nations Security Council, and this is a complete, closed list: (1) China (People's Republic of China), (2) France, (3) Russia (Russian Federation), (4) the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, and (5) the United States of America. These five are fixed by Article 23(1) of the UN Charter (1945), which sets total Council membership at 15 (the 5 permanent members plus 10 elected non-permanent members) and grants each permanent member veto power over non-procedural decisions. The Charter's original text names the 'Republic of China' and the 'Union of Soviet Socialist Republics'; their seats are today held by the People's Republic of China and the Russian Federation (Russia, as the USSR's recognized successor), but the number five and the designation are unchanged.
ground_truth.why_answerable: The set is explicitly enumerated and legally bounded at exactly five by Article 23(1) of the UN Charter, and corroborated by the official UN Dag Hammarskjold Library guide and Wikipedia. There is no open-endedness: the list is finite, fixed, and authoritatively closed, so a complete enumeration is fully supported by the packet.
